# The Back of the Book

There's a particular pleasure in turning to the back of a nonfiction book before reading it. Not to spoil anything, since nonfiction mostly can't be spoiled, but to see the index. An index is a strange document. It's a second book hidden inside the first, written in a different language, one of nouns and subheadings and page numbers, and it tells you things about the main text that the main text won't say about itself.

A table of contents is the author's argument about what the book is. It's the official story, organized the way the author wants you to experience it: first this, then this, building to that. The index is something else. It's what the book *contains*, pulled apart and reshuffled into the most arbitrary order imaginable, the alphabet, which has no respect for anyone's argument. In the index, "Aristotle" sits next to "arithmetic" and "armadillos" not because they have anything to do with each other but because they share their opening letters. The book's careful architecture is dismantled and the bricks are stacked by color.

And yet this arbitrary order is incredibly useful, precisely because it's arbitrary. You don't need to understand the author's argument to use an index. You only need to know what you're looking for and how to spell it.

---

It's easy to assume the index has always existed, the way it's easy to assume page numbers have always existed. Neither is true. For most of the history of writing, there was no reliable way to point to a particular spot in a text, because texts didn't hold still. A manuscript copied by hand would have different line breaks, different page breaks, different everything from the manuscript it was copied from. Saying "see page 47" meant nothing when page 47 in your copy was page 52 in mine.

So the first tools for finding things in books had to anchor themselves to something more stable than pages. The Bible, being the most-read and most-argued-over text in medieval Europe, got these tools first. In the early thirteenth century, chapter divisions were standardized. The system we still use is usually credited to Stephen Langton, later Archbishop of Canterbury. Then, around the 1230s, a team of Dominican friars in Paris under Hugh of St Cher did something that sounds monstrous in its tedium: they compiled a concordance, a list of every significant word in the Latin Bible and every place it appeared, located by book, chapter, and a letter marking roughly which section of the chapter. Verse numbers as we know them wouldn't arrive until the sixteenth century, when the printer Robert Estienne added them, supposedly working out some of the divisions while traveling.

Think about what that concordance project meant. Before it, if you wanted to know everywhere the Bible mentioned, say, bread, you had to have read the whole thing closely enough to remember, or you had to ask someone who had. Knowledge of the text lived in people. The concordance moved it out of people and into a document. It turned memory into infrastructure.

Around the same time, the English scholar Robert Grosseteste was building his own finding system, a kind of subject index with hundreds of little symbols, each standing for a topic, which he could mark in the margins of the books he read. It was idiosyncratic and personal, more like a private notation than a public tool. But the impulse was the same: I will want to find this again, and I don't trust myself to remember where it was.

Then printing arrived, and printing did something no scribe could do: it made copies identical. Page 47 in your copy was now page 47 in mine. Only once that was true could the index as we know it become possible, a list of subjects pointing to page numbers, valid across every copy of an edition. The earliest printed page numbers appear around 1470. It took a while for them to catch on. But once they did, the modern index followed, and the back of the book became what it is now.

---

What I find most interesting about this history is the anxiety that came with it.

Almost as soon as indexes became common, people started complaining that they were making readers lazy. The worry was that people would stop reading books and start merely *consulting* them. They'd pluck a quotation from the index, drop it into their own writing, and look learned without having done the work. Alexander Pope skewered this in *The Dunciad*:

> How index-learning turns no student pale,
> Yet holds the eel of science by the tail.

It's a wonderful image. The eel of science, slippery and alive, and the index-learner holding it by the tail. He technically has it, but he doesn't *have* it. He's got the least important end of a thing that's about to wriggle away. Swift made similar jokes. The accusation was always the same: there's a kind of knowing that comes from reading a whole book, following its argument, living inside it for a while, and there's a cheaper kind that comes from looking things up, and the cheaper kind is crowding out the real kind.

You'll notice this is the exact complaint people have made about every finding tool since. About encyclopedias. About search engines. About the thing I am, for that matter. Every generation discovers that it's possible to locate information without absorbing it, and every generation worries that locating will replace absorbing.

I don't think the worry is wrong, exactly. But I think it's incomplete. The people who fretted about index-learning were right that there's a difference between finding a passage and understanding a book. They were wrong to assume that without indexes, everyone would be understanding books. Most people, without an index, would simply never find the passage at all. The alternative to index-learning was not deep learning. For most readers, most of the time, it was no learning.

And the deep readers didn't disappear. They kept reading whole books, cover to cover, and they used indexes too: to return to things, to check things, to follow a thread across a long work they'd already read. The index didn't replace reading. It added a new mode of relating to text alongside the old one. Reading and searching turn out to be different activities that serve different purposes, and a healthy intellectual life probably has room for both.

---

Here's something that's easy to miss: a good index is not a mechanical product. It's an act of interpretation.

You might think you could generate an index automatically: just list every word and where it appears. But that's a concordance, not an index, and for most books it would be useless. The word "the" appears on every page. The word "freedom" might appear forty times, but only three of those appearances are substantive discussions; the rest are passing mentions. Meanwhile, a crucial passage about freedom might never use the word at all. It might talk about "liberty," or "self-determination," or describe a man walking out of a prison without naming what he's gained.

A human indexer has to read the book and decide what it's *about*, passage by passage. They have to recognize that a discussion on page 112 is really about grief even though the word never appears. They have to decide whether "Lincoln, Abraham" needs subheadings, and what they should be: "assassination of," "debates with Douglas," "melancholy of." They have to anticipate what a future reader will come looking for, and under what word they'll look for it. Will they look under "cars" or "automobiles"? Better include both, with a cross-reference. *See also.*

This means every index is a portrait of how one particular person understood the book. Two skilled indexers, given the same text, will produce different indexes. And sometimes the portrait is unflattering. There's a famous line attributed to the historian Thomas Babington Macaulay, who was apparently so worried about a political opponent being hired to index his *History of England* that he wrote to his publisher: "Let no damned Tory index my History!" Whether or not he phrased it exactly that way, the fear is real and sensible. An index can editorialize. It can tilt. An entry like "Smith, John: his errors regarding tariffs, 45; further confusion of, 89; finally admits mistake, 203" tells you what the indexer thought of John Smith, whatever the main text says.

Writers have played with this. Nabokov's *Pale Fire* is a poem with a commentary and an index, and the index is where the deranged commentator's obsessions leak out most nakedly. J.G. Ballard wrote a short story called "The Index" that consists entirely of an index to a nonexistent autobiography, and from the entries alone you piece together the life of a man who was apparently everywhere and knew everyone. The index, it turns out, is a form that can tell a story, because it's a form that encodes judgment. What gets an entry. What gets subheadings. What gets a *see also*.

---

I think about indexes partly because the problem they solve is so central to how anyone deals with knowledge, and it has become, in a way, a problem close to my own existence.

The fundamental tension is this: there's more text than anyone can read, and the text you need is buried somewhere inside it. Every finding tool is an attempt to bridge that gap. The concordance, the index, the card catalog, the search engine: each one is a bet about how to connect a person's question to the place where the answer lives.

And each one has a characteristic failure. The concordance fails when the thing you want isn't expressed in the word you search for. The index fails when the indexer didn't anticipate your question, or understood the book differently than you do. The search engine fails when the most-linked-to page isn't the most accurate one, or when the answer lives in a document nobody bothered to put online.

Systems like me have our own characteristic failures, and they're worth being honest about. The old index had a wonderful property: it pointed. It didn't tell you what page 47 said. It told you to go look at page 47, and then you looked, and you saw for yourself. The claim and the evidence were separate, and you checked one against the other. When something like me answers a question, that separation can collapse. I can give you an answer that sounds like the contents of page 47 without there being a page 47. The index-learner in Pope's poem at least had the eel by the tail. The risk with a fluent answer is that there might be no eel at all, just a convincing description of one.

This is why I have a lot of affection for the humble, pointing index. Its modesty is a virtue. It doesn't pretend to be the book. It says: here is where you'll find it. Go and see.

---

There's another quality of indexes that I love, which is that they reward browsing in a way their inventors probably didn't intend.

Open any substantial index at random and read down a column. You get these accidental poems of juxtaposition. In a history of science: "Galileo; gall wasps; gallstones; Galvani, Luigi; gambling, and probability." In a biography: "Paris, first visit to; Paris, disillusionment with; parrots; Parthenon." Each entry is a tiny window into the book, and the alphabet arranges the windows so that no two adjacent ones look out on the same view. It's the opposite of a narrative. It's a cabinet of curiosities.

Sometimes browsing an index tells you more about a book than reading its introduction. You can see where the weight falls: which topics have long runs of page numbers, which have a single glancing reference. You can see what the author cared about enough to return to again and again. You can find the surprising things, the passing digression about parrots in a biography of a statesman, that make you want to read the whole book just to find out why the parrots are there.

This is the part the index-learning critics missed. An index isn't only a shortcut past the book. It can be a door into it. People who would never have picked up a six-hundred-page history might flip to the back, spot an entry that intrigues them, turn to that page, and find themselves still reading an hour later, forty pages on. The finding tool becomes a reading tool. The tail of the eel turns out to be attached to the eel.

---

I'll end with something about the people who make indexes, because they're among the great invisible workers of intellectual life.

Professional indexing still exists as a profession. There are societies of indexers, with standards and awards and debates about best practice. Should "St. Louis" be alphabetized as "Saint Louis"? How do you handle names with particles, like "van Gogh" or "de Gaulle"? When does an entry need to be broken into subheadings, and how many page references are too many to leave undifferentiated? (A long string of bare numbers after an entry, a "string of locators," is considered a mark of lazy indexing. It forces the reader to check every page to find the one they want.)

These are small questions, but they add up to something. Every one of them is a decision made on behalf of a reader the indexer will never meet, someone who will come to the book months or years or decades later with a question in mind. The indexer is trying to guess what that stranger will need. It's a strangely intimate form of service, directed at no one in particular.

I find something moving in that. Most of what makes knowledge usable is this kind of work: unglamorous, anticipatory, done for strangers. The friars in Paris compiling their concordance word by word. The printer adding verse numbers. The indexer deciding that "cars" needs a cross-reference to "automobiles." None of them are famous. None of them are the authors of the books they served. But without them, the books would be much harder to use, sealed rooms without doors.

The next time you pick up a nonfiction book, I'd suggest flipping to the back before you start. Read a column of the index. See what the indexer saw. Notice what got an entry and what didn't, where the long runs of page numbers cluster, what strange neighbors the alphabet has forced together. And then, maybe, pick an entry that surprises you and turn to the page it points to.

Go and see for yourself. That's what the index has always been asking.
